hero.title: Kolabr vs Basecamp
hero.lede: Basecamp keeps a tidy list of what each project needs doing. Kolabr runs the whole client relationship as it happens: the conversation, requests with an owner and a clock your guests can see, calls started from the work they are about, a wiki that answers before anyone asks, and a channel that carries on long after one project ends.

tuesday.title: The same Tuesday, in each
tuesday.lede: One client, one ordinary day. Both tools can carry it. Watch where the work lives, and who has to remember what.

steps.basecamp: The client posts on the project’s message board. Someone reads it later and writes a to-do with an assignee and a due date.

kolabr.title: The message becomes request #418
kolabr.text: One step turns it into a numbered request with an owner, a category and a four-hour response target, and your guests can see all three.

steps.basecamp: A quick call would settle it. Basecamp’s features list has no video calls, so someone pastes a link to a separate video tool into the chat.

kolabr.title: The call starts from the request
kolabr.text: Screen sharing, a whiteboard over the shared screen and a recording, and the call stays linked to #418 so the decision is with the work.

steps.basecamp: The to-do has a due date, so it turns overdue once the date passes. Until then, nothing says it is slipping.

kolabr.title: It shows as at risk before it is late
kolabr.text: The response target is running down, so the request is marked at risk on the channel dashboard while there is still time to act.

steps.basecamp: A new guest from the client asks how invoicing works. Someone types the answer again, or digs through last year’s archived project for it.

kolabr.title: The wiki answers first
kolabr.text: They start raising a request and the channel wiki suggests the article on invoicing before they finish typing.

beyond.title: What a to-do list was never built to do
beyond.lede: All of this is on Kolabr Pro, in every channel, with no other subscription to add.

tiles.title: Live, not checked later
tiles.body: Chat with presence, threads and voice notes. Calls start from the request they are about, with screen sharing, a whiteboard over the shared screen and a recording kept for 30 days.

tiles.title: A clock your guests can see
tiles.body: Every request has an owner, a category and a response target, and your guests see all three. Routing sends it to the right person as it arrives.

tiles.title: The channel remembers
tiles.body: A wiki in every channel, with version history, readable by your guests and suggested to a guest while they are asking.

tiles.title: Repeat work runs itself
tiles.body: Onboarding, a monthly report, a round of revisions: deploy a playbook and the steps, owners and due dates are filled in for you. Automation rules and recurring events take care of the rest.

tiles.title: The relationship never closes
tiles.body: One channel holds every job you do for that client, year after year. Nobody is re-invited, and nothing is archived away from the conversation that produced it.

tiles.title: Room for every client
tiles.body: Channels are unlimited on both paid plans, and so are guests. Your fortieth client adds nothing to the bill, the same as your fourth.

statement.title: Built around the client, not the project
paragraphs: Basecamp is shaped around projects, and it is good at them: a project opens, the work gets done, the project is archived. Client work rarely ends that neatly. A retainer, a support contract or a six-year relationship produces a new project every few months, and the history ends up split across all of them.

A Kolabr channel is the relationship itself. Guests join once and stay. Work arrives as requests, closes, and is still there in two years next to the wiki article that explains how you handled it. A big job can still have its own channel; the client’s history does not have to start again when it does.

cost.title: What you pay for, plan by plan
cost.lede: Basecamp charges one fee for the whole account, and every plan has the same tools, so moving up buys room: more active projects and more storage. Kolabr charges for users, and moving up buys capability. Channels and guests are unlimited on both paid plans, whatever the size of your client list.

same.title: The same tools on every plan
same.text: Message boards, to-dos, card tables, Campfire chat, a schedule, docs and files, and check-ins. Upgrading changes the limits, not what you can do.

same.text: Unlimited channels and unlimited free guests, with no project limit. Your fortieth client costs what your fourth did: nothing.

items.title: Does Kolabr replace Basecamp’s to-dos?
items.body: For client work, yes. What you would put on a to-do becomes a request: numbered, with an owner, a category and a response target your guests can see, and a checklist of tasks inside it when the work has steps. What Kolabr does not have yet is a board view, so if your team plans work as cards moving across columns, keep that where it is for now.

items.title: We would hit Basecamp’s project limit. What happens on Kolabr?
items.body: Nothing changes. Channels are unlimited on both paid plans, so a channel per client, or several, never moves the price. The bill follows your team, not how busy your year is.

items.title: Both have free clients, so what is the difference?
items.body: What your guests walk into. In Basecamp a client is invited to a project and sees its message board, to-dos and schedule. In Kolabr your guests have a channel where they talk to you live, raise requests and watch the clock on them, join calls and read the wiki, and it is the same channel for every piece of work you do together.

items.title: Which is cheaper?
items.body: Basecamp, while you run a few projects at a time: $59 a month covers ten active projects for any number of people. Past twenty-five active projects Basecamp is $299 a month billed yearly, where a team of twelve on Kolabr Pro pays $102 a month on yearly terms. Either way, the question worth asking is what the money buys: a to-do list per project, or requests with a clock, calls, a wiki and playbooks in every client’s channel.

items.title: What about ongoing work that never really ends?
items.body: This is the common reason firms outgrow a project-shaped tool. Support, retainers, maintenance and standing client relationships have no finish date, so they sit uneasily in something built around projects. A Kolabr channel has no end date, and requests come and go inside it.

items.title: Can we move from Basecamp to Kolabr?
items.body: Yes, and the usual approach is to stop creating new projects rather than migrate old ones. Open a channel for your busiest client, run the next piece of work there, and let the Basecamp archive stay readable for as long as you need it.

proof.title: Proof takes one week
proof.lede: Take your longest-standing client, the one whose work never really stops. No project has to be closed and nothing has to be exported.

steps.text: Open one channel for that client and invite everyone on their side. Guests cost nothing, so there is no list to approve first.
The whole relationship is in one place, and every open item has a name and a date on it instead of sitting in a list somebody has to remember to check.
You will know from the client whether a channel beats a project. That is the only test this page is asking you to run.

cta.title: Give the relationship a home.
cta.body: Free for one channel, no card. Seven days on Pro or Business when you want the rest. Start with the client whose work never really finishes.
